summary.heading: Isotopes and the strong nuclear force
summary.html:
• Isotopes: same number of protons, different numbers of neutrons (e.g. carbon-12, -13, -14). Some are stable, some radioactive.
  • Protons repel strongly at nuclear distances, and gravity is far too weak to hold them together.
  • The strong nuclear force acts between all nucleons (p–p, p–n, n–n). It is attractive, very strong and short-range (up to about $3 \times 10^{-15}$ m); repulsive below about $0.5 \times 10^{-15}$ m, which stops nucleons merging.
  • Each nucleon is held only by its nearest neighbours, but the electric repulsion acts between every pair of protons, so large nuclei need extra neutrons.
  • The guide spells it out: an attractive force must balance the protons' repulsion; it has a very short range; it acts on protons and neutrons, not electrons.
  • HL New for 2028 Its range is of order $10^{-15}$ m, about the size of a nucleon.

summary.heading: Mass defect and binding energy
summary.html:
$$E = mc^2$$
  • Mass defect $\Delta m$: the mass of the separate nucleons minus the mass of the nucleus (always positive).
  • Binding energy: the energy needed to separate a nucleus completely into its nucleons (= energy released when it forms), $E = \Delta m\,c^2$.
  • Mass units: kg; $1\ \text{u} = 1.661 \times 10^{-27}$ kg; $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}\,c^{-2}$ (multiply a mass in u by 931.5 to get MeV).
  • In any nuclear reaction, energy released = (mass before − mass after) $\times c^2$. Energy is released only if the products have less mass. Keep all the decimal places when subtracting masses.

summary.heading: Binding energy per nucleon
summary.html:
• Measures how tightly each nucleon is held: higher means more stable.
  • Rises steeply for light nuclei (helium-4 unusually high), peaks near iron and nickel ($A \approx 56$–62, about 8.8 MeV), then falls gradually as the protons' repulsion grows.
  • Reactions that move nuclei up the curve release energy: fusion of light nuclei (E.5) and fission of heavy ones (E.4).
  • Total binding energy = binding energy per nucleon × $A$.
  • HL Above $A \approx 60$ the curve is roughly constant (7.5–8.8 MeV): evidence that the strong force is short-range.

summary.heading: Radioactive decay: alpha, beta and gamma
summary.html:
• Decay is random (can't predict when a given nucleus decays; each has the same chance in a given time) and spontaneous (unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemistry).
  • Nucleon number and charge are conserved in every decay equation.
DecayWhat happensChange
αemits $^{4}_{2}\alpha$ (heavy nuclei)$A - 4$, $Z - 2$
β⁻n → p; emits electron + antineutrino $\bar{\nu}_e$ (too many neutrons)$A$ same, $Z + 1$
β⁺p → n; emits positron + neutrino $\nu_e$ (too many protons)$A$ same, $Z - 1$
γexcited nucleus drops to a lower state, emits a photonno change
  • Neutrinos and antineutrinos: no charge, almost no mass, hardly interact with matter. They are needed to conserve energy and momentum in beta decay.

summary.heading: Penetration and ionization
summary.html:
NatureIonizingStopped byIn fields

βelectron or positronmediuma few mm of aluminium; up to about 1 m of airdeflected strongly

  • The more strongly a radiation ionizes, the faster it loses energy and the shorter its range.
  • Alpha is least dangerous outside the body, most dangerous inside it.

summary.heading: Activity, count rate and half-life
summary.html:
• Activity $A$: decays per second, in becquerels (1 Bq = 1 decay per second). Count rate: what the detector records, always less than the activity.
  • Half-life $T_{1/2}$: the time for the number of undecayed nuclei, or the activity, to halve. Fixed for each nuclide, whatever the starting amount.
  • After $n$ half-lives the fraction left is $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^n$ (whole numbers of half-lives at SL). Watch whether a question asks for the fraction left or the fraction decayed.
  • Background radiation (radon, cosmic rays, rocks and buildings, food, medical sources): measure it first over a long time and subtract it from every reading. Only the source's count rate halves.
  • Measuring a half-life: record the count rate at regular intervals, correct for background, plot it against time, read off several halving times and average.

summary.heading: Using radioactivity
summary.html:
• The choice of isotope depends on its radiation (penetration) and its half-life.
  • Medical tracers: a gamma emitter with a half-life of hours (technetium-99m, 6 h).
  • Leaks in underground pipes: a short-half-life gamma emitter added to the fluid.
  • Thickness control: beta for paper and thin plastic, gamma for thick steel; long half-life so the count rate changes only with thickness.
  • Dating: carbon-14 (5730 years) for once-living material up to about 50 000 years; uranium-238 or potassium-40 for rocks.

summary.heading: Evidence for the strong force and nuclear stability
summary.html:
• Evidence for the strong force: nuclei exist despite the protons' repulsion; deviations from Rutherford scattering at high energies (E.1); constant nuclear density and a roughly constant binding energy per nucleon above $A \approx 60$ (short range).
  • Band of stability ($N$ against $Z$): light stable nuclei have $\frac{N}{Z} \approx 1$; heavy ones need more neutrons ($\frac{N}{Z} \approx 1.5$ for lead-208). Nothing beyond $Z = 83$ is stable.
  • Above the band (too many neutrons): β⁻. Below it (too many protons): β⁺. Very heavy nuclides: alpha decay.

summary.heading: Nuclear energy levels and the neutrino
summary.html:
• Alpha particles from one nuclide have a few definite energies, and gamma rays a few definite photon energies (a line spectrum): evidence for discrete nuclear energy levels, spaced by MeV (about a million times atomic levels).
  • Beta particles have a continuous spectrum from almost zero up to a maximum equal to the energy released. With only two products, momentum conservation would give the electron one energy every time.
  • So a third particle, the (anti)neutrino, shares the energy: the continuous beta spectrum is the evidence for the neutrino.

summary.heading: The decay law and the decay constant
summary.html:
$$N = N_0e^{-\lambda t} \qquad A = \lambda N = \lambda N_0e^{-\lambda t} \qquad T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$
  • Decay constant $\lambda$ (unit $\text{s}^{-1}$, $\text{h}^{-1}$, $\text{y}^{-1}$…): the rate of decay is proportional to $N$. Works for any time, not just whole half-lives.
  • $\lambda\Delta t$ approximates the probability that a nucleus decays in a short time $\Delta t$, but only when $\lambda t \ll 1$ (over one half-life $\lambda t = 0.693$ but the probability is 0.5).
  • To find $t$: $t = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}\ln\dfrac{N_0}{N}$. A graph of $\ln A$ (or $\ln N$) against $t$ is a straight line of gradient $-\lambda$.
  • Number of nuclei in a sample: mass ÷ (nucleon number × $u$). For an activity in Bq, $\lambda$ must be in $\text{s}^{-1}$.

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Calling binding energy energy "stored" in the nucleus: it is the energy needed to pull it apart.
  • Forgetting the (anti)neutrino, or swapping them: β⁻ antineutrino, β⁺ neutrino.
  • Changing $A$ or $Z$ in gamma decay.
  • Thinking a sample loses half its mass in one half-life: the daughter nuclei are still there.
  • Halving the count rate before removing the background.
  • Thinking it is all gone after two half-lives (a quarter is left), or that heating speeds up decay.
  • HL Mixing time units for $\lambda$ and $t$; using $\log_{10}$ instead of $\ln$; saying the beta spectrum shows energy isn't conserved; saying β⁺ happens in neutron-rich nuclei.

Serendipity: Becquerel's discovery was an accident, but what did he do afterwards that made it science?
"Chance favours the prepared mind." What preparation did Becquerel and the Curies need to recognize what they had found?
Conservation laws: Faced with the beta spectrum, some physicists (including Bohr) were ready to give up energy conservation. Why did Pauli's alternative win?
How strong should our confidence in a conservation law be? What would it take to abandon one?
Risk: Radium tonics and glowing watch dials: why were the dangers missed for so long?
The same gamma rays cause cancer and treat it. How do doctors decide when the benefit outweighs the risk?
Patterns: Roll a large set of dice, removing every six each round. Why is the class total predictable when no single die is?
Where else does a predictable pattern come from many random events (gas pressure, insurance, election polls)?

oracy.html:
ABC discussion (threes, 8 minutes): each student in turn agrees with, builds on or challenges the last point. Claim: "An isotope's half-life is 10 minutes. A single nucleus of it hasn't decayed after 30 minutes, so it is overdue and more likely than ever to decay in the next 10."

  • I agree with … because …
  • Building on that, …
  • I'd challenge that, because …

Listen for: decay is random and spontaneous, so a nucleus has no memory of its age; the probability that it decays in the next half-life is still one half.

Can a random process be a law of nature?: Is "each nucleus has a fixed chance of decaying per second" a law about nuclei or a statement about our ignorance?
Compare the decay law with Newton's second law. Is one more certain than the other?
Should we believe in what we can't detec: Pauli worried he had proposed a particle that could never be detected. Was belief in the neutrino before 1956 scientific?
Students believe in many things they can't detect themselves. What makes that belief justified?
Who decides what risk is acceptable?: Smoke detectors contain americium-241. Should every household have been asked before they were sold?
Do experts and the public measure risk in the same way? What else, besides probability, matters to people?
How far can we extrapolate?: What independent evidence could support the assumption that half-lives were the same millions of years ago?
Carbon dating needs a calibration curve. What does that tell us about the limits of a single method?
